items.stem: Explain how the writer uses sentence structure for effect in this extract: ‘Slowly, carefully, without making a sound, Tariq lifted the latch.’
items.answer: The fronted adverbs and phrase delay the main action, mirroring Tariq’s slow, careful movement and building suspense.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies sentence type(s)/structure; effect on pace, tension or emphasis; credit for developed explanation with reference.

items.stem: Identify the technique used in ‘I did not speak in class for a month.’ (an autobiography extract, ‘Arrival’) and analyse its effect on the reader.
items.answer: Short sentence (‘I did not speak in class for a month.’): the plain sentence emphasises the writer’s isolation and silence.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (short sentence); 1 for selecting the key words ‘I did not speak in class for a month.’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. the plain sentence emphasises the writer’s isolation and silence.

items.stem: Explain why each paragraph of an argument should begin with a clear topic sentence.
items.answer: The topic sentence tells the reader the point of the paragraph, helping them follow the line of argument.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: signals the point; clarity of structure.

items.stem: Read ‘JAMIE: It was already like this! I just... wanted to see it.’ from an extract from a play, ‘The Clock’. Name the language feature, quote the key words and explain how they shape the reader’s response.
items.answer: Ellipsis (‘I just... wanted’): the hesitation reveals Jamie’s vulnerable feelings about his grandfather.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (ellipsis); 1 for selecting the key words ‘I just... wanted’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. the hesitation reveals Jamie’s vulnerable feelings about his grandfather.

items.stem: Read this transcript: ‘Thank you, Mateo. I agree with your point about safety, but I wonder whether the cost might be a problem. Ines, what do you think?’ Write feedback for the speaker giving one strength, one weakness and two specific improvements, with reasons.
items.answer: Strengths: acknowledges the previous speaker, builds on the idea, raises a counter-point politely, invites others to speak. Improvements: A model of good discussion; could add evidence about the cost.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: valid strength; valid weakness; two specific, practical improvements; reasons linked to the audience.

items.stem: Line from the poem ‘Harbour at Dawn’: ‘Gulls stitch the sky with silver thread’ Line from the poem ‘City Rain’: ‘A taxi hisses past.’ Explain one similarity or difference in the way these two lines create an effect.
items.answer: The first uses metaphor, whereas the second uses onomatopoeia: the gulls’ flight paths become threads sewn across the sky, suggesting delicate, criss-crossing movement and light catching their wings. By contrast/similarly, the hissing sound of tyres on wet roads is captured exactly, and the short line mirrors the quick passing.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying the technique in each line; 1 for a comparative point about effect; credit any valid comparison.

items.stem: What is the climax of a story?
options: The moment of greatest tension or the turning point
items.answer: The moment of greatest tension or the turning point
items.markingKey: Everything builds to it; afterwards tension falls.

items.stem: Why do information texts often use subheadings?
options: To organise the information so readers can find what they need
To tell a story in order
items.answer: To organise the information so readers can find what they need
items.markingKey: Subheadings divide content into topics and help skimming and scanning.

items.stem: Read this narrator’s account: ‘I am not a nosy person. I just happen to notice things, such as the fact that Mr Dube’s curtains have been closed for four days, which I have written in my notebook.’ Explain why the reader might not trust this narrator.
items.answer: The narrator denies being nosy but records neighbours’ curtains in a notebook, so their self-description cannot be trusted.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies the gap between what the narrator claims and what the evidence shows; quotes the revealing detail; credit for explaining the effect (humour, sympathy or suspicion).

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence with correct punctuation and capital letters: ‘the twins jake and ella are starting secondary school’
items.answer: Model: ‘The twins, Jake and Ella, are starting secondary school.’
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: capital letters; correct clause punctuation; apostrophes and speech marks where needed. Accept equivalent correct versions (e.g. a full stop instead of a semicolon).

items.stem: Read a memoir extract, ‘The River’. ‘I learned to swim in the brown river behind my uncle’s house the summer I was nine. There was no teacher, no float, no shallow end; there was only my cousin Bilal, who was eleven and therefore an expert. “Just kick,” he said, and let go of my hands. I sank like a stone. Under the water everything turned green and silent, and I remember thinking, quite calmly, that this was a strange place to end up. Then Bilal’s hand closed around my collar and hauled me into the air. I coughed half the river onto the bank. “Again,” he said. Looking back now, I am amazed that either of us was allowed near that water. But by the end of August I could swim to the far bank and back, and I have never since felt quite so proud.’ (a) Who taught the writer to swim? (b) Look at ‘who was eleven and therefore an expert’. How does the writer create humour here? (c) The writer writes ‘I coughed half the river onto the bank.’. Identify the technique and explain its effect. (d) How does the writer present the experience of learning to swim?
items.answer: (a) Their cousin Bilal (b) The adult writer gently mocks the child’s belief that being two years older made Bilal an expert; ‘therefore’ makes the logic sound comically serious. (c) Hyperbole: the exaggeration is comic and shows how much water the child swallowed. (d) Humorous, affectionate tone; Bilal as a comic, determined teacher; vivid sensory moment underwater; hyperbole; adult reflection (Looking back now); pride at the end.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: Their cousin Bilal [1] (b) 1 mark: irony/gentle mockery; 1 mark: explains ‘therefore’ or the age gap [2] (c) 1 mark technique (hyperbole); 2 marks explanation of effect, e.g. the exaggeration is comic and shows how much water the child swallowed. [3] (d) Level-marked: top band (3–4) perceptive analysis with precise references; middle (2) clear explanation of some effects; lower (1) mainly retelling. [4]

items.stem: Analyse how the writer uses language in these two quotations from a student’s speech to the school council, ‘Give Us a Quiet Room’: (i) ‘Where did you go?’ (ii) ‘A recent survey of our Year 9 found that seven out of ten students feel stressed during exam season.’ Identify a technique in each and explain its effect.
items.answer: (i) Rhetorical question: the question makes listeners recall their own frustration, so they relate to the problem. (ii) Statistic: the figure provides evidence and makes the problem seem widespread rather than personal.
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks from: for each quotation, 1 for the technique (rhetorical question; statistic) and 1 for an explanation of its effect; remaining mark(s) for a developed point linking both to the mood or purpose of the text.

items.stem: Read an extract from a play, ‘The Interview’. ‘A small office. A desk, two chairs. MS RAO, the manager, is typing. NADIA (17) stands in the doorway, clutching a folder. MS RAO: (not looking up) Sit. (NADIA sits on the edge of the chair. She drops the folder; papers scatter. She scrambles to collect them.) NADIA: Sorry. Sorry, I— MS RAO: Why do you want to work here? NADIA: (taking a deep breath) Because my mother worked here. For twenty years. Until you let her go. (MS RAO stops typing. A long silence.) MS RAO: (slowly) Does she know you’ve come? NADIA: No. (MS RAO closes the laptop.)’ (a) What is Ms Rao doing at the start of the scene? (b) Look at ‘She drops the folder; papers scatter. She scrambles to collect them.’. What does this action show about Nadia’s state of mind? (c) How does the playwright show the change in the relationship between Ms Rao and Nadia?
items.answer: (a) Typing (b) She is extremely nervous; the clumsy action shows she is under pressure and not in control. (c) Ms Rao dominant at first (not looking up, ‘Sit’); Nadia nervous (dropped folder, repeated ‘Sorry’); revelation in short sentences; silence; Ms Rao’s slow question and closing laptop show power shifting.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: Typing [1] (b) 1 mark: nervous; 1 mark: links the action to her feelings [2] (c) Level-marked: top band (7–9) perceptive analysis with precise references; middle (4–6) clear explanation of some effects; lower (1–3) mainly retelling. [9]

items.stem: Read a newspaper opinion column, ‘Skate Park Plan Is a Disaster Waiting to Happen’: ‘The council’s plan to build a skate park beside Jubilee Gardens is, quite simply, madness. The gardens are one of the last peaceful places in our town, loved by families, pensioners and wildlife alike. Now the council wants to fill them with concrete ramps and teenagers shouting at all hours. The park will cost $250,000. Local residents were consulted in a survey last spring, but only 300 people replied. Everyone I have spoken to is against it. Supporters claim the park will keep young people off the streets, but in my experience bored teenagers will cause trouble wherever they are. The council should listen to the people who actually pay for it, before it is too late.’ How does the writer try to shape the reader’s response? Consider word choice, quotation and the order of information.
items.answer: Word choice and connotations; use and placement of quotations; facts and figures; opening and ending; balance or bias; overall effect on readers’ attitudes.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (reading). Top band (7–10): perceptive, well-developed analysis of how the writer uses language and structure to create effects; precise, well-chosen references; sustained focus on the question; middle band (4–6): clear explanation of some effects with relevant references; some analysis of particular words and phrases; lower band (1–3): some relevant points, mostly retelling the text; few references; little comment on language. Indicative content: Word choice and connotations; use and placement of quotations; facts and figures; opening and ending; balance or bias; overall effect on readers’ attitudes.

items.stem: Write one original line of poetry that uses metaphor to describe a city at midnight. Then explain the effect you intended.
items.answer: Any original metaphor about a city at midnight, e.g. ‘The station was a beehive of hurrying people.’ with an explanation of the mood or picture created.
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks from: 1 for an accurate metaphor; 1 for originality/aptness (not a cliché); remaining mark(s) for explaining the intended effect.

items.stem: Rewrite the extract from ‘The Mill’ as a modern story opening set in the present day, keeping the irony but using contemporary language. Write about 350–450 words.
items.answer: Model approach: modern vocabulary and syntax; same ironic narrator; Josiah updated (e.g. a silent neighbour); comparison of how the style has changed.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 12: Content and structure 7 marks, Style and accuracy 5 marks. items.stem: Read the two paragraphs. A: ‘Why Leaves Change Colour’ ‘In autumn, the leaves of many trees turn from green to red, orange and yellow. The green colour comes from chlorophyll, which plants use to capture sunlight. As days shorten and temperatures fall, trees stop making chlorophyll. The green fades, revealing yellow and orange pigments that were there all along. Some trees also produce new red pigments. Eventually the leaves fall, helping the tree save water through winter.’ B: ‘Sleep and Teenagers’ ‘Teenagers need between eight and ten hours of sleep a night, yet many get far less. During puberty, the body clock shifts, so teenagers naturally feel sleepy later in the evening. Early school starts and late-night screen use make the problem worse, because the blue light from phones delays the release of melatonin, the hormone that makes us sleepy. Lack of sleep can affect memory, mood and concentration.’ Summarise the key information from both paragraphs as a short paragraph for a school science display. Use your own words; about 100–120 words.
items.answer: A: In autumn, shorter, colder days stop trees producing green chlorophyll, revealing hidden yellow and orange pigments and sometimes new red ones, before the leaves fall. B: Many teenagers sleep less than the eight to ten hours they need because their body clocks shift later, school starts early and screens delay melatonin, harming memory and mood.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): all or nearly all relevant points identified; expressed concisely in own words; well organised and within the word limit; middle band (3–4): most relevant points; mostly own words; some repetition or unnecessary detail; lower band (1–2): few relevant points; much copying or irrelevant detail; may exceed the limit. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: A – shorter days/colder weather; chlorophyll production stops; hidden yellow/orange pigments revealed; some make red pigments. B – body clock shifts later; early school starts; screens delay melatonin. Register: clear, factual, formal.

items.stem: Write the opening of a story called ‘The Stranger on the Platform’ that uses the weather or setting to suggest the main character’s mood. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model approach for ‘The Stranger on the Platform’: begin with a precise image or action, introduce the main character through what they do, plant one unanswered question, and end the section at a moment of tension. Pathetic fallacy; atmosphere linked to feeling; controlled description.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): setting, character and tension all established quickly and subtly; a strong hook; detail selected to raise questions the reader wants answered; middle band (3–4): setting and character introduced with some effective detail; some attempt to create interest or tension; lower band (1–2): a basic introduction that tells rather than shows; little sense of setting or tension. items.stem: Explain the effect of this line from a poem: ‘Sweet, deep sleep will keep you till the dawn’
items.answer: the long ‘ee’ sounds are soothing and drawn-out, like a lullaby.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘Sweet, deep sleep will keep you till the dawn’. Model point: the long ‘ee’ sounds are soothing and drawn-out, like a lullaby. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: Identify the technique used in ‘Dada Farouk’s stall was the smallest in the market, but people queued for it anyway.’ (an extract from a story, ‘The Radio Mender’) and analyse its effect on the reader.
items.answer: Contrast (‘the smallest in the market, but people queued’): the contrast between the tiny stall and the queue shows that his reputation and skill matter more than appearances.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (contrast); 1 for selecting the key words ‘the smallest in the market, but people queued’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. the contrast between the tiny stall and the queue shows that his reputation and skill matter more than appearances.

items.stem: Use the context to explain what ‘Pray’ means in ‘Pray write soon’, and suggest a modern word or phrase that could replace it.
items.answer: Please. A modern replacement: Please.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: accurate meaning; suitable modern equivalent that fits the sentence.

items.stem: Read an extract from a comedy, ‘Stage Fright’: ‘A school stage, the night of the play. Behind the curtain. OMAR, dressed as a tree, paces. OMAR: (to the audience) Twelve lines. I have twelve lines and I can remember precisely none of them. (Enter MRS CHEN, the director, with a clipboard.) MRS CHEN: Omar! Places, please. Two minutes. OMAR: Mrs Chen, I think I’ve got a fever. MRS CHEN: (feeling his forehead) You’ve got stage fright. Everybody has it. Even trees. (She exits. OMAR takes a deep breath and turns to face the curtain. It begins to rise.) OMAR: (whispering) Here goes.’ Identify three conventions of a playscript used in this extract and explain how each helps a director or actor.
items.answer: E.g. setting description at the start (helps design the stage); character names before lines (shows who speaks); stage directions in brackets (how to move or speak, e.g. pauses, props, lighting); entrances and exits; sound or lighting cues.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 per convention correctly identified with an example; further marks for explaining its use in performance.

items.stem: Here is a student’s draft explanation: ‘The bread rises. You mix flour, water and yeast. The yeast makes gas. You bake it. You leave it somewhere warm.’ Rewrite this explanation so that it is clear, in the right order and uses connectives.
items.answer: First, flour, water and yeast are mixed to make dough. The dough is then left somewhere warm, where the yeast feeds and produces carbon dioxide gas. As a result, the dough rises. Finally, it is baked.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: Award for: correct sequence; time and causal connectives; impersonal style; technical term (carbon dioxide). Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: In a recount, the writer revises ‘We moved house when I was ten. I went to a new school.’ into ‘We moved house when I was ten, and although I hated the new school at first, I can see now that it taught me how to make friends from nothing.’ How does this change help the reader understand the experience?
items.answer: It turns a bare event into a meaningful memory: the older writer looks back and explains what the experience taught them, so the reader understands its significance.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: shows hindsight or a change in understanding; explains the significance or lesson of the event; links past and present self.

items.stem: Why do reporters include quotations from witnesses?
options: To add credibility and human interest
items.answer: To add credibility and human interest
items.markingKey: Quotes give real voices and evidence.

items.stem: Which feature is typical of formal writing?
options: Full forms such as ‘do not’ instead of ‘don’t’
items.answer: Full forms such as ‘do not’ instead of ‘don’t’
items.markingKey: Formal writing avoids contractions and slang.

items.stem: Explain the effect of the words ‘members of the council, teachers and fellow students’ in this line from a student’s speech to the school council, ‘Give Us a Quiet Room’: ‘Good morning, members of the council, teachers and fellow students.’
items.answer: greeting each group shows respect and awareness of a mixed, formal audience, and establishes a polite, confident tone.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘members of the council, teachers and fellow students’. Model point: greeting each group shows respect and awareness of a mixed, formal audience, and establishes a polite, confident tone. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: Identify the structural feature in these lines and analyse why the poet might have used it: ‘Rain arrives in the city / without knocking.’
items.answer: Enjambment: the line break holds back ‘without knocking’, giving it surprise, like the rain itself.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for enjambment; remaining marks for an analysis that links the structure to meaning or mood.

items.stem: Read the opening of a story, ‘Nobody Believes Me’. ‘I want to make it clear from the start that I did not break the greenhouse. Everyone in our street thinks I did, including my mother, who has known me for thirteen years and should frankly know better. Yes, I was in the garden. Yes, I had the cricket bat. And yes, the ball did happen to be lying among the broken glass when Mr Okoro came running out in his slippers. But anyone who has studied physics, which I have, for nearly a whole term, knows that a ball cannot travel that far on its own. Someone else was involved. Possibly a fox. I explained all this to Mr Okoro, calmly and reasonably, while he made a noise like a kettle coming to the boil.’ How does the writer make the narrator seem unreliable and humorous? Support your answer with close reference to the text.
items.answer: Admits all the evidence; repetition of ‘Yes’; exaggerated expertise; absurd fox excuse; ironic ‘calmly and reasonably’; mocking simile about Mr Okoro.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (reading). Top band (7–10): perceptive, well-developed analysis of how the writer uses language and structure to create effects; precise, well-chosen references; sustained focus on the question; middle band (4–6): clear explanation of some effects with relevant references; some analysis of particular words and phrases; lower band (1–3): some relevant points, mostly retelling the text; few references; little comment on language. Indicative content: Admits all the evidence; repetition of ‘Yes’; exaggerated expertise; absurd fox excuse; ironic ‘calmly and reasonably’; mocking simile about Mr Okoro.

items.stem: These events from a story plan are in the wrong order. A: Arjun is chosen to read a poem at assembly. B: He practises but grows more nervous each day. C: Arjun finishes the poem and is cheered. D: A friend in the front row mouths the first line. E: On stage, his mind goes blank in front of the whole school. Put them in the order of a story mountain and label each stage.
items.answer: ABEDC: exposition (opening) – Arjun is chosen to read a poem at assembly.; rising action – He practises but grows more nervous each day.; climax – On stage, his mind goes blank in front of the whole school.; falling action – A friend in the front row mouths the first line.; resolution – Arjun finishes the poem and is cheered.
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks from: correct order ABEDC; labels exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution.

items.stem: Read an extract from a play, ‘The Clock’: ‘A cluttered attic. Evening. Rain against the window. JAMIE (14) kneels beside an open trunk. Enter TARA (16), holding a torch. TARA: What are you doing up here? JAMIE: (without turning) Nothing. TARA: That’s Grandad’s trunk. Mum said— JAMIE: I know what Mum said. (He lifts out a small brass clock. Its glass is cracked.) TARA: (quietly) You broke it. JAMIE: It was already like this! I just... wanted to see it. (Pause. TARA sits on the floor beside him. She takes the clock gently.) TARA: He used to wind it every Sunday. Said it was the only thing in the house that never lied. (Thunder. The torch flickers and goes out. Darkness.) JAMIE: Tara?’ Continue the scene from the moment the torch goes out, revealing what Jamie really feels about Grandad and building to a new moment of tension. Use playscript conventions. Write about 350–450 words.
items.answer: Model approach: darkness used for confession; Tara’s response; a sound or discovery that raises tension; stage directions for lighting and movement.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 12: Content and structure 7 marks, Style and accuracy 5 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–7): correct playscript layout throughout; dialogue reveals character and motivation and builds tension; stage directions purposeful; a clear shape to the scene; middle band (3–4): mostly correct layout; dialogue gives some sense of character; some stage directions; scene has a beginning and end; lower band (1–2): layout often incorrect; dialogue flat or confusing; few stage directions. Style and accuracy – top band (4–5): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2–3): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: darkness used for confession; Tara’s response; a sound or discovery that raises tension; stage directions for lighting and movement. Characters’ motivations remain consistent with the extract.

items.stem: Read an information leaflet, ‘Mangroves: The Coast’s Living Wall’. ‘Mangroves are trees that grow where the land meets the sea. Unlike most plants, they can survive in salty water, and their tangled roots arch out of the mud like the legs of a giant spider. These roots do far more than hold the trees up. They slow down waves and trap sediment, protecting coastlines from erosion and storm surges. They also shelter young fish, crabs and shrimps, which is why mangroves are often called the nurseries of the sea. Mangrove forests store large amounts of carbon in their soil, helping to slow climate change. Sadly, large areas of mangrove have been lost in recent decades, much of it cleared for shrimp farms and coastal building. Visitors can help by staying on boardwalks, taking litter home and supporting local replanting projects.’ (a) Look at ‘These roots do far more than hold the trees up.’. What is the purpose of this sentence in the leaflet? (b) The writer writes ‘their tangled roots arch out of the mud like the legs of a giant spider’. Identify the technique and explain its effect. (c) How does the leaflet inform readers and also encourage them to protect mangroves?
items.answer: (a) It is a topic sentence that signals a shift from describing the roots to explaining their wider benefits, making the reader expect a list of uses. (b) Simile: the vivid comparison helps the reader picture the arching, many-legged roots, making the information memorable. (c) Definition; vivid simile of spider legs; list of benefits; metaphor nurseries of the sea; carbon fact; ‘Sadly’ signals concern; practical advice to visitors ends with a call to action.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: signals/introduces new information; 1 mark: leads into the benefits that follow [2] (b) 1 mark technique (simile); 2 marks explanation of effect, e.g. the vivid comparison helps the reader picture the arching, many-legged roots, making the information memorable. [3] (c) Level-marked: top band (4–5) perceptive analysis with precise references; middle (2–3) clear explanation of some effects; lower (1) mainly retelling. [5]

items.stem: Identify the type of life writing in this extract, explain the features that show it, and rewrite the sentence as a different type (e.g. biography into autobiography): ‘Throughout his career, the architect insisted on visiting every building site personally, according to colleagues.’
items.answer: Biography: third person and uses others’ accounts as sources. The rewrite should change person and/or tense and tone appropriately.
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks from: 1 for the type (biography); 1 for supporting features; remaining mark(s) for an accurate rewrite in a different form.

items.stem: Write an article for your school magazine persuading students to walk or cycle to school. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model structure: hook (question or striking fact); problem; two or three reasons with evidence and emotive detail; counter-argument rebutted; call to action.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): a clear, sustained point of view; well-developed reasons supported by evidence; counter-arguments anticipated and rebutted; logical, cohesive paragraphs and a strong conclusion; middle band (3–4): a clear view with some supporting reasons and evidence; some development; paragraphs mostly logical; lower band (1–2): a simple view with few or undeveloped reasons; limited organisation. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: clear persuasive purpose; a range of techniques (rhetorical question, rule of three, emotive language, statistics, direct address, counter-argument); structured paragraphs; strong call to action.

items.stem: In an extract from a story, ‘The Platform’ the writer writes: ‘when the sound drifts up from the valley, and suddenly she is eight again’ How does the writer move from the present into the past?
items.answer: The sound of the whistle triggers the memory; ‘suddenly’ shows the abrupt shift, and the tense stays present to make the memory vivid.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: trigger (whistle); ‘suddenly’/abrupt transition

items.stem: Use these notes to write a headline and an opening paragraph (lead) for a news report aimed at local students. Notes: Saturday; Riverside School robotics team (4 students, aged 13–14); won national schools robotics final in Kuala Lumpur; robot sorts recycling; beat 32 teams; captain Aisha Rahman: “We failed three times before it worked”; prize: trip to world championships in Tokyo.
items.answer: Model: a short, striking headline; a lead of one or two sentences answering who, what, where, when and why, in the past tense and third person, with language suited to the audience.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for an effective headline; 1–2 for covering the 5 Ws accurately; 1 for register suited to local students.

items.stem: In the sentence ‘The old house was big.’, the word ‘big’ could be replaced by ‘vast’ or ‘rambling’. Explain how each choice changes the meaning or effect.
items.answer: ‘vast’ and ‘rambling’ each give a more specific picture than ‘big’; a precise adjective suggests the shape and atmosphere of the house.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for the connotation of ‘vast’; 1 for ‘rambling’; further mark for comparing effects.

items.stem: Read an explanation text, ‘How a Solar Still Works’. ‘A solar still is a simple device that uses the sun’s heat to turn salty or dirty water into clean drinking water. First, a shallow basin is filled with the untreated water and covered with a sloping sheet of clear plastic or glass. Sunlight passes through the cover and warms the water, causing some of it to evaporate. The water vapour leaves salt, mud and most germs behind. When the vapour touches the cooler underside of the cover, it condenses into droplets. Because the cover slopes, these droplets run down into a collecting channel and then into a container. A small still might produce only a few litres a day, but it needs no fuel, no electricity and very little maintenance, which makes it valuable in remote, sunny places.’ Identify 2 features that show this is an explanation text, giving an example of each and explaining its purpose.
items.answer: Possible features: present tense for general truths; technical vocabulary; causal and sequencing connectives (e.g. ‘As a result’, ‘First’, ‘Because’); impersonal third-person style; a clear opening that introduces the topic.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: for each feature, 1 for the feature with an example from the text; credit purpose (clarity, sequence, accuracy, authority).

items.stem: Write a five-paragraph plan for a balanced argument answering the question ‘Should the school day start later?’ Give a one-line summary of each paragraph.
items.answer: Model plan: 1 Introduction – the issue and why it matters; 2 Arguments for, with evidence; 3 Arguments against, with evidence; 4 Weighing the strongest points / possible compromise; 5 Conclusion – reasoned judgement.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: introduction; points for; points against; evaluation; conclusion with judgement; logical order.

items.stem: In a short scene, an actor follows the stage direction (He grips the back of the chair until his knuckles whiten.) What does this action show the audience?
items.answer: The tight grip shows he is struggling to control anger or fear.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: a valid inference about the character’s feelings or situation linked to the action, e.g. the tight grip shows he is struggling to control anger or fear.

items.stem: Read ‘I did not speak in class for a month.’ (an autobiography extract, ‘Arrival’). Which language feature does the writer use here?
items.answer: Short sentence
items.markingKey: Short sentence: a deliberately brief sentence that stands out. Here ‘I did not speak in class for a month.’ – the plain sentence emphasises the writer’s isolation and silence.

items.stem: What does ‘in medias res’ mean?
options: Starting in the middle of the action
items.answer: Starting in the middle of the action
items.markingKey: Latin for ‘into the middle of things’: the story begins at an exciting point.

items.stem: Explain the effect of this line from a poem: ‘The slow black slug slid silently across the step.’
items.answer: the repeated ‘s’ sounds imitate the slug’s quiet, slippery movement.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘The slow black slug slid silently across the step.’. Model point: the repeated ‘s’ sounds imitate the slug’s quiet, slippery movement. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence in modern English, keeping the meaning. ‘It was upon a raw evening in the latter part of November that I first beheld the house at Thornleigh.’
items.answer: Model: ‘I first saw the house at Thornleigh on a cold, damp evening late in November.’
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: Award for accurate meaning; archaic words replaced; natural modern syntax. Accept any version that meets the instruction and keeps the meaning; deduct for new errors.

items.stem: Read a persuasive article from a school magazine, ‘Ditch the Plastic Bottle’: ‘Every day, our school throws away more than four hundred plastic bottles. Four hundred! Imagine them piled in the playground: a glittering mountain of waste that will outlive every one of us. Is that really the legacy we want to leave? Some people say that recycling solves the problem, but only a small fraction of all the plastic ever made has been recycled. The rest is buried, burned or washed into the sea, where it chokes turtles and breaks down into tiny fragments that end up in the fish we eat. The solution is simple, cheap and fair: install free water fountains and give every student a refillable bottle. Other schools in our city have already done it. We can do it too, and we must start now.’ How does the writer use language and structure to influence the reader’s view of the people and events?
items.answer: Word choice and connotations; use and placement of quotations; facts and figures; opening and ending; balance or bias; overall effect on readers’ attitudes.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10 (reading). Top band (7–10): perceptive, well-developed analysis of how the writer uses language and structure to create effects; precise, well-chosen references; sustained focus on the question; middle band (4–6): clear explanation of some effects with relevant references; some analysis of particular words and phrases; lower band (1–3): some relevant points, mostly retelling the text; few references; little comment on language. Indicative content: Word choice and connotations; use and placement of quotations; facts and figures; opening and ending; balance or bias; overall effect on readers’ attitudes.

items.stem: Rewrite this sentence so that it begins with a prepositional phrase (e.g. ‘Beneath the bridge,…’, ‘In the morning,…’): ‘The market filled with noise at dawn.’
items.answer: Model: ‘At dawn, the market filled with noise.’
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks from: begins with a prepositional phrase; meaning kept; correctly punctuated (comma after the opening element).

items.stem: Read an information leaflet, ‘Mangroves: The Coast’s Living Wall’. ‘Mangroves are trees that grow where the land meets the sea. Unlike most plants, they can survive in salty water, and their tangled roots arch out of the mud like the legs of a giant spider. These roots do far more than hold the trees up. They slow down waves and trap sediment, protecting coastlines from erosion and storm surges. They also shelter young fish, crabs and shrimps, which is why mangroves are often called the nurseries of the sea. Mangrove forests store large amounts of carbon in their soil, helping to slow climate change. Sadly, large areas of mangrove have been lost in recent decades, much of it cleared for shrimp farms and coastal building. Visitors can help by staying on boardwalks, taking litter home and supporting local replanting projects.’ (a) Which is one way the leaflet says visitors can help? (b) Look at ‘Sadly, large areas of mangrove have been lost in recent decades’. What does the word ‘Sadly’ show about the writer’s attitude? (c) How does the leaflet inform readers and also encourage them to protect mangroves?
items.answer: (a) Taking their litter home (b) The writer is not completely neutral: ‘Sadly’ expresses regret and encourages the reader to care about protecting mangroves. (c) Definition; vivid simile of spider legs; list of benefits; metaphor nurseries of the sea; carbon fact; ‘Sadly’ signals concern; practical advice to visitors ends with a call to action.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: Taking their litter home [1] (b) 1 mark: regret/concern; 1 mark: effect on reader (to persuade them to help) [2] (c) Level-marked: top band (7–9) perceptive analysis with precise references; middle (4–6) clear explanation of some effects; lower (1–3) mainly retelling. [9]

items.stem: Write a letter to your headteacher persuading them to create a school garden. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model structure: hook (question or striking fact); problem; two or three reasons with evidence and emotive detail; counter-argument rebutted; call to action.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): form and register fully appropriate (greeting, purpose stated early, sign-off); points developed and well ordered; tone consistently suited to the reader; middle band (3–4): recognisable letter form; points clear with some development; tone mostly suitable; lower band (1–2): form inconsistent; points brief or unclear; tone unsuited to the reader. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: clear persuasive purpose; a range of techniques (rhetorical question, rule of three, emotive language, statistics, direct address, counter-argument); structured paragraphs; strong call to action.

items.stem: Analyse how the writer uses language in these two quotations from an extract from a play, ‘The Clock’: (i) ‘TARA: That’s Grandad’s trunk. Mum said— JAMIE: I know what Mum said.’ (ii) ‘JAMIE: It was already like this! I just... wanted to see it.’ Identify a technique in each and explain its effect.
items.answer: (i) Dialogue: the interruption shows conflict between the siblings and Jamie’s defensiveness, raising tension. (ii) Ellipsis: the hesitation reveals Jamie’s vulnerable feelings about his grandfather.
items.markingKey: Award up to 10 marks from: for each quotation, 1 for the technique (dialogue; ellipsis) and 1 for an explanation of its effect; remaining mark(s) for a developed point linking both to the mood or purpose of the text.

items.stem: Write a memoir about a mistake that taught you something important. Include vivid detail of the experience and reflection on what it meant to you. Write about 350–450 words.
items.answer: Model structure: opening at a vivid moment; context; the key incident with sensory detail and dialogue; turning point; reflection (‘Looking back…’) on what a mistake that taught you something important taught you.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 12: Content and structure 7 marks, Style and accuracy 5 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–7): a vivid, selective account with a clear chronology; reflection on the significance of the experience woven in; a distinctive personal voice; middle band (3–4): a clear account with some detail and some reflection; personal voice present; lower band (1–2): a list of events with little detail or reflection. Style and accuracy – top band (4–5): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2–3): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: focused, selected moments; sensory detail; remembered dialogue; reflective comments showing hindsight; ending that links past to present.

items.stem: Write a scene in which two friends argue about a secret, revealing their characters through dialogue and action rather than direct description. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Plan: setting (bus stop after school); Friend A hints she knows; Friend B deflects with jokes; tension rises; B finally admits the truth; final gesture shows the friendship may survive.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): an engaging, well-developed story with a clear, controlled structure; convincing characters and setting; tension or interest sustained; an effective ending; middle band (3–4): a clear story with some development of character and setting; structure mostly secure but pace may be uneven; lower band (1–2): a simple sequence of events with little development; structure unclear or ending abrupt. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: Distinct voices for each friend; actions and gestures that show emotion; subtext; a turning point; correct dialogue punctuation.

items.stem: Write a poem of three stanzas about a place you know well at three different times of day, using enjambment at least twice. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model features: three stanzas with a clear time sequence; enjambment for effect; a final turn or reflection.
items.markingKey: Level-marked out of 10: Content and structure 6 marks, Style and accuracy 4 marks. Content and structure – top band (5–6): form handled deliberately and accurately; structural choices (stanzas, line breaks, rhyme) clearly linked to meaning; middle band (3–4): recognisable form with some deliberate choices; lower band (1–2): form loosely followed; little sense of structure. Style and accuracy – top band (3–4): precise, often ambitious vocabulary chosen for effect; a wide range of sentence structures used deliberately; register consistently suited to audience and purpose; spelling, punctuation and grammar almost always accurate; middle band (2): generally appropriate vocabulary with some ambition; some variety of sentence structure; register mostly suitable; occasional errors that do not obscure meaning; lower band (1): simple or repetitive vocabulary; limited sentence variety; register may slip; frequent errors in spelling, punctuation or grammar that sometimes obscure meaning. Indicative content: three stanzas with a clear time sequence; enjambment for effect; a final turn or reflection.
